Evidentiary Requirements for Property Ownership in Inheritance Division In a lawsuit for the judicial dissolution of an inheritance community involving land and rural buildings, the plaintiffs requested the sale of the assets, while the defendant argued for a division in kind. The legal classification concerns the burden of proof (onus probandi) regarding the deceased's ownership of the estate. The interpretative challenge lies in determining whether fiscal or administrative documentation is sufficient to prove property rights. The Court applied the principle that cadastral surveys and inheritance tax returns do not constitute proof of ownership. Cadastral data has purely fiscal relevance, and the tax return is a unilateral declaration that does not verify the actual legal transfer of property. Consequently, the failure to produce the original title of acquisition leads to the rejection of the division claim.
Limits of the Non-Contestation Principle in Property Rights The litigation was characterized by the parties' mutual agreement regarding the composition of the inheritance mass, as the defendant did not contest the ownership of the assets. This involves the legal application of the non-contestation principle under Art. 115 c.p.c.. The interpretative problem is whether the court can proceed with a division based solely on the parties' consensus in the absence of formal titles. The Court ruled that in property division cases, the judge must verify that the assets are effectively and objectively owned by the parties, rather than merely "undisputedly" owned. The lack of contestation cannot heal the absence of legal proof of ownership, as the court is prohibited from dividing assets whose membership in the estate is not strictly documented.
